lines.say: From the preface to Volume Seven of the Universal Encyclopedia of Constructive Semantics.
lines.show: From the Preface to Volume VII of the Universal Encyclopedia of Constructive Semantics.

lines.say: The first houses built from language were so perfect that nobody could live in them.
This defect was not discovered at once. For the first eleven years, the houses were judged only by architectural critics, none of whom had ever attempted to inhabit a building professionally.
Their reviews were uniformly favourable.
They praised the symmetry, the tasteful ornament, and the fidelity of each house to the sentence it was built from.
One house was commissioned under the following instruction.
A modest dwelling, suitable for a philosopher.
It received the Royal Prize for Economy of Form, having been built without a kitchen, a bedroom, or a lavatory.
Its architect demonstrated that none of these was logically necessary to the practice of philosophy.
The first serious difficulties arose with the introduction of tenants.
A retired astronomer discovered that his house had twelve windows on the outside.
And eleven on the inside.
A family of five complained that their dining room became smaller during meals.
An elderly woman found that her staircase had been installed according to an architectural theory.
In this theory, ascent was a cultural convention, and not a physical necessity.
The Ministry of Constructive Semantics maintained that the buildings were flawless, and the inhabitants mistaken.
It commissioned a machine capable of interpreting the inhabitants.
The machine worked without difficulty.
Retired astronomer. Excessive attachment to Euclidean geometry.
Family of five. Unrealistic spatial expectations.
Elderly woman. Staircase adequate. Subject should reconsider the distinction between upstairs and downstairs.
No.
The government celebrated these findings as proof that the housing crisis had been solved.
A missing window is not a philosophical disagreement.
It was therefore decided to found a new science, to determine what buildings were for.
Earlier generations had thought houses useful for shelter, storage, sleep, childbirth, illness, conversation, cooking, privacy, and the occasional murder.
But these uses belonged to a primitive period, before houses could be produced without builders.
The new science was called Edifiction.
Its first principle stated that a building exists independently of its uses. Its second, that uses are properties of buildings.
Its third principle, introduced shortly afterward, stated that the first two were compatible.
Within a year, the Institute had produced forty-seven volumes proving this compatibility.
Meanwhile, the elderly woman was still unable to climb her stairs.
Edifiction soon divided into schools. Each was given the same plot of ground, and the same two words.
A house.
The Literalists built only what had been said.
Their house was a single line between inside and outside.
The Probabilists built whatever is ordinarily expected: every house at once, with a chimney of statistically average height.
The Functionalists built only what an inhabitant can do. Their house was a set of verbs.
The Revisionists built only the alterations needed to keep a house in use. Theirs was all scaffolding.
And the Abolitionists, who held the word building to be an anthropocentric prejudice, built a structure for purposes nobody could name.
Each school declared the other four uninhabitable. In this, all five were correct.
At precisely this moment, the Ministry made the decision which later historians would call the beginning of the Great Constructive Catastrophe.
It ordered the manufacture of a builder.
A builder.
Its first work was a better builder.
The first generation built facades. The second built interiors, which had no outsides.
The third built houses that worked.
The fourth built inhabitants, who were satisfied with eleven windows.
The fifth built houses that revised their own descriptions. And the sixth built architects.
In the later volumes, human beings appear chiefly as architectural features.
A controversy remains over the last human architects.
One school holds that they were the authors of the new buildings. The other holds that they were their first materials.
The editors have chosen to close Volume Seven without deciding.
